image.proof_notes: Commons file 'File:Giethoorn Canal 1.jpg' confirms Giethoorn; desc: Giethoorn, Dutch Venice

facts.one_liner: Canal village in Weerribben-Wieden; ~2,800 residents, car-free historic core, boatable waterways.
facts.why_go: Giethoorn is a living village in Overijssel’s Kop van Overijssel, often called Hollands Venetië for its canals, thatched farmhouses, and wooden bridges. Visitors come to explore by whisper boat, bike, or on foot rather than through a museum gate. The old centre has no through car traffic; lakes nearby were formed by historic peat digging. Boat rental needs no licence, but advance booking is strongly advised on busy days.
facts.best_time: May–September for boating and long daylight; arrive before 10:00 or after 16:00 for quieter canals. Shoulder months April and October are milder and less crowded.
facts.how_to_get_there: No station in the village. Train to Steenwijk, then bus 70 or seasonal Giethoorn Express (270) to Hylkemaweg–Giethoorn Centre / Hollands Venetië. By car, park on the P-route at the edge; the centre is car-free. About 10 minutes’ drive from Steenwijk, 30 from Zwolle.
facts.good_to_know: It is a lived-in village (~2,600–2,800 people), not a theme park—stay off private gardens and paths. No entrance fee to walk the village.

facts.one_liner: Rif mountain town (~600 m) known as Chaouen; blue-washed medina, Kasbah, and hiking access.
facts.why_go: Chefchaouen (also Chaouen / شفشاون) sits in Morocco’s western Rif between Tétouan and Ouazzane. People come for the blue-and-white medina lanes, Place Outa Hammam with the Kasbah museum, and day hikes toward Akchour and Talassemtane National Park. The medina’s Andalusian-influenced layout and mountain setting distinguish it from larger imperial cities. Early morning and late afternoon give better light and fewer day-trippers.
facts.best_time: April–May and September–October for mild days and clearer hiking conditions. July–August are warmer and busier with domestic weekend traffic; winter is quieter but cooler and wetter.
facts.how_to_get_there: Most visitors arrive by bus or shared grand taxi from Tangier, Tétouan, or Fès (mountain roads; allow several hours). No train station—use CTM/local coaches into the new town, then walk or taxi into the medina.
facts.good_to_know: Dress modestly in the medina; ask before photographing residents. Pair the town with a guided hike rather than relying only on street photos—Ras el-Maa and the Spanish Mosque viewpoint are short walks from the old quarter.

image.attribution: Photo: chensiyuan, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
image.proof_notes: Commons file 'File:1 hallstatt austria.jpg' confirms Hallstatt; desc: hallstatt austria unesco

facts.one_liner: Lakeside market town on Hallstätter See; UNESCO Hallstatt–Dachstein/Salzkammergut core, salt-mine heritage.
facts.why_go: Hallstatt is a small municipality on the southwest shore of Lake Hallstatt beneath the Dachstein massif in Upper Austria. Visitors come for the lakeside old town, salt-mine and museum history (the Hallstatt culture name originates here), the Skywalk above the roofs, and the Beinhaus ossuary. The settlement sits on a narrow strip between cliff and water, so most exploration is on foot. Day-trip pressure is high; staying overnight or arriving very early changes the experience.
facts.best_time: May–June and September–October for milder weather and fewer peak crowds. July–August and sunny weekends see heavy day tourism; winter is quieter with snow possible.
facts.how_to_get_there: Train via ÖBB to Attnang-Puchheim, then Salzkammergut Railway to Hallstatt station on the opposite shore; ferry (~15 min) to the village pier. From Salzburg, bus 150 to Bad Ischl, then local buses (change at Gosaumühle for Hallstatt Lahn). By car, Austrian motorway vignette required; village parking is scarce—book ahead or travel early.
facts.good_to_know: Tour buses are time-slot limited; overnight guests get preference. Village centre parking is largely for residents—plan public transport or reserved lots.

image.attribution: Photo: --sinava-- from Berlin, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

facts.one_liner: Alsatian prefecture city; half-timbered old town, Petite Venise canals, and Alsace Wine Route hub.
facts.why_go: Colmar (Alsatian: Colmer) is the Haut-Rhin prefecture between the Vosges and the Rhine, known as a capital of Alsace wines. Travellers come for the protected historic centre—Petite Venise, the Tanner’s quarter, Maison Pfister, Maison des Têtes—and the Unterlinden Museum with the Isenheim Altarpiece. The pedestrian core mixes French and Germanic architecture across several centuries. It works as a base for the Route des Vins and nearby villages.
facts.best_time: May–June and September–October for walking weather and vineyard season. December Christmas markets are popular but crowded; July–August are peak summer.
facts.how_to_get_there: Gare de Colmar has frequent TER/TGV-linked trains from Strasbourg and Mulhouse. Nearest major airports: Basel–Mulhouse–Freiburg (~52 km) and Strasbourg (~68 km). Town centre is walkable from the station; tourist office at Place Unterlinden.
facts.good_to_know: Old-town lighting is strongest Friday–Saturday evenings year-round and nightly during major events (wine fair, Christmas). The tourist office stocks maps of Petite Venise and museum tickets info.

image.author: Orlando Paride
image.attribution: Photo: Orlando Paride, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
image.proof_notes: Commons file 'File:Civita (Bagnoregio) - Panorama.jpg' confirms Civita di Bagnoregio; desc: Civita (Bagnoregio) - Panorama

facts.one_liner: Cliff-top borgo above the Valle dei Calanchi; footbridge-only access from Bagnoregio, ticketed entry.
facts.why_go: Civita di Bagnoregio is a frazione of Bagnoregio in Tuscia, perched on friable tuff above clay badlands. Visitors cross a reinforced pedestrian bridge into a compact medieval street plan with Etruscan roots, San Donato church, and calanchi views. Ongoing erosion earned it the nickname “la città che muore,” so the setting itself is part of the visit. Only a handful of permanent residents remain; day tourism is the main activity.
facts.best_time: April–June and September–October for cooler bridge climbs. Avoid midday heat in July–August; early morning or late evening are more comfortable and less crowded.
facts.how_to_get_there: A1 exit Orvieto (~18 km) or Attigliano (~30 km) to Bagnoregio. Park at Piazzale Battaglini; shuttle or ~1.3 km walk to the Belvedere, then cross the ~300 m bridge on foot. Train to Orvieto or Viterbo, then COTRAL bus to Bagnoregio. Online ticket holders go straight to the bridge entrance.
facts.good_to_know: Entry is ticketed (managed by Casa Civita); the bridge climb is steep—unsuitable in peak heat for anyone with heart/mobility issues. Bikes are not allowed into the village.

image.author: lumoplank
image.attribution: Photo: lumoplank, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons
image.proof_notes: Commons file 'File:Shirakawa-go - Shirakawa156.jpg' confirms Shirakawa-go; desc: Interior of a traditional gassho-zukuri farmhouse, showing the steep thatched roof framework bound with rope.

facts.one_liner: Ogimachi gasshō-zukuri village (白川郷); UNESCO Historic Villages of Shirakawa-go and Gokayama.
facts.why_go: Shirakawa-gō’s Ogimachi hamlet in Shirakawa Village (Gifu) preserves steep thatched gasshō-zukuri farmhouses adapted to heavy snow. Together with Gokayama sites in Toyama it forms a UNESCO World Heritage property inscribed in 1995. Visitors walk the village lanes, climb to the observatory overlook, and optionally stay in farmhouse lodgings. Several houses operate as museums explaining silk-raising and roof construction; many remain private homes.
facts.best_time: Late April–May (greenery), mid-October (foliage/Doburoku Festival period), and winter for snow scenery if roads and clothing are prepared. Golden Week and autumn festival dates bring congestion.
facts.how_to_get_there: No passenger rail in the village. Highway buses (reservations often required) from Takayama (~50 min), Kanazawa (~75 min), or Nagoya. By car use village Seseragi Park Parking, then cross Deai Bridge; vehicle entry into the World Heritage core is restricted. Winter driving needs studless tires or chains.
facts.good_to_know: Use official Seseragi parking—not private touts near the entrance. Respect residents: many buildings are homes, and fire risk is high in thatched clusters.

image.proof_notes: Commons file 'File:Sidi Chebaan.jpg' confirms Sidi Bou Said; desc: the beautiful coffe "Sidi Chebaan" in sidi bousaid with one of the best views in the world :)

facts.one_liner: Cliff suburb ~20 km NE of Tunis; white walls, blue shutters, Gulf of Tunis views (سيدي بو سعيد).
facts.why_go: Sidi Bou Saïd overlooks the Gulf of Tunis on a steep promontory, known for Andalusian-style houses in white and cobalt blue. Visitors stroll Rue Hedi Zarrouk and side lanes, stop at cliff cafés, and visit Dar Ennejma Ezzahra (Centre of Arab and Mediterranean Music) or house museums such as Dar el-Annabi. It pairs easily with Carthage ruins a few kilometres west. The upper village is compact and mostly pedestrian.
facts.best_time: Spring and autumn for mild weather and thinner crowds than peak summer. Arrive before 11:00 or stay overnight for quieter streets; afternoons draw day-trippers.
facts.how_to_get_there: TGM suburban train from Tunis Marine toward La Marsa; alight at Sidi Bou Saïd station (~0.5 km below the centre), then walk uphill. Taxis/rideshares drop near Rue Hedi Zarrouk. Combine with Carthage on the same TGM line.
facts.good_to_know: During Ramadan many daytime food stalls close—plan iftar or eat outside fasting hours. The marina is reached via the steep “365 Steps” (fewer in practice); upper streets are the main photo circuit.

image.attribution: Photo: Pudelek, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
image.proof_notes: Commons file 'File:Čičmany - wooden houses.jpg' confirms Čičmany; desc: Čičmany, village in Slovakia

facts.one_liner: Mountain village in Rajecká dolina; log houses with white geometric wall patterns (folk architecture reserve).
facts.why_go: Čičmany lies in Žilina District between the Strážovské vrchy and Malá Fatra, famous for timber houses painted with distinctive white ornaments. A folk architecture reserve (declared 1977) protects a cluster of these houses; Radenov dom and House No. 42 hold Považské múzeum ethnographic displays on daily life, dress, and crafts. Patterns also appear in local embroidery. The village itself remains small and residential.
facts.best_time: May–September for open-air wandering and museum hours; July–August have the longest museum days. Winter is atmospheric but cold and services thinner.
facts.how_to_get_there: By car via Rajecká Lesná / Rajecké Teplice area south of Žilina (mountain valley roads). Public transport is limited—check Žilina regional buses toward Čičmany and confirm return times. Museum address: Čičmany 137.
facts.good_to_know: Museum closed Mondays; Tue–Fri roughly 9:00–15:00 with a midday break, longer on weekends—confirm current hours on pmza.sk before going. Walk the lower village respectfully; many painted houses are private homes.

image.attribution: Photo: Frokor, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
image.proof_notes: Commons file 'File:Reine, Lofoten.jpg' confirms Reine; desc: Reine i Lofoten ein sommarkveld i 2007

facts.one_liner: Fishing village on Moskenesøya; Moskenes municipal centre, Arctic Circle, E10 access, ~300 residents.
facts.why_go: Reine sits between Vestfjorden and Reinefjorden on Moskenesøya in the Lofoten archipelago. People come for harbour and peak views, rorbu cabins, stockfish racks, and hikes such as Reinebringen (stone staircase built 2016–2019). It remains a working fish-processing community, not only a viewpoint. Neighbouring Hamnøy and Å are short hops along the same road.
facts.best_time: June–August for hiking, ferries, and midnight sun. May and September are quieter with long daylight. October–March for Northern Lights potential, but expect short days, limited services, and hazardous winter trails.
facts.how_to_get_there: Ferry Bodø–Moskenes, then bus/taxi to Reine; or fly to Leknes or Svolvær and continue by bus/car on E10. Check Reis Nordland (reisnordland.com / Reis app) for bus 300 / Lofotekspressen and local links. Public parking in the village—streets are narrow.
facts.good_to_know: Reinebringen is strongly discouraged in winter for safety. Respect active fishery work and do not handle drying stockfish; use marked campsites only.

image.author: Diego Delso
image.attribution: Photo: Diego Delso, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
image.proof_notes: Commons file 'File:Albarracín, Teruel, España, 2014-01-10, DD 034.JPG' confirms Albarracín; desc: Albarracín, Teruel, Spain

facts.one_liner: Pink-walled hill town in a Guadalaviar meander; Sierra de Albarracín, Monumento Nacional since 1961.
facts.why_go: Albarracín climbs a rocky loop of the Guadalaviar at about 1,180 m in southern Aragón. Visitors walk the medieval street maze, cathedral and walls (Torre del Andador views), and pinkish sandstone façades. The surrounding sierra offers walking and the Rodeno pine/boulder landscape popular with climbers. It is capital of the Sierra de Albarracín comarca and a member of Spain’s Most Beautiful Villages association.
facts.best_time: May–June and September–October for comfortable walking and autumn colour in the sierra. Summers are warm by day with cooler nights; winters can bring snow and quieter streets.
facts.how_to_get_there: Best by car: ~2 h from Valencia (A-23), ~3 h from Madrid, ~5 h from Barcelona. Bus link from Teruel bus station typically Mon–Sat (e.g. Teruel 08:50 / Albarracín 14:10 on municipal info—confirm current times). Limited Sunday/holiday service.
facts.good_to_know: Use designated parking outside the historic core; streets are very narrow. Check albarracin.es or Albarracín Movilidad for up-to-date bus tickets before relying on a same-day connection from Teruel.

image.author: Bgabel
image.attribution: Photo: Bgabel, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
image.proof_notes: Commons file 'File:NZL-waitomo-cave-exit.jpg' confirms Waitomo Glowworm Cave exit; desc: Exit of the Waitomo glowworm cave

facts.one_liner: Guided limestone caves with a silent boat ride under Arachnocampa luminosa glowworms.
facts.why_go: The Waitomo Glowworm Caves are a show-cave complex in rural Waikato where guided tours walk through chambers such as the Cathedral before a short boat ride through the glowworm grotto. Discover Waitomo operates the official Glowworm Cave alongside nearby Ruakuri and Aranui caves, so the area works as a half-day or multi-cave stop between Auckland and Rotorua. Expect cool, damp underground conditions and a cashless visitor centre at 39 Waitomo Village Road.
facts.best_time: Year-round; summer (Dec–Feb) has longer daylight and more departures, while shoulder months (Mar–May, Sep–Nov) are quieter. Book ahead in school holidays.
facts.how_to_get_there: About 1 hour by road from Hamilton, ~2.5 hours from Auckland. Drive via SH3/SH37 to Waitomo Village, or join day tours from Auckland/Rotorua. Tours check in at the Glowworm Caves Visitor Centre.
facts.good_to_know: Pre-booking online via Discover Waitomo is essential; check in 30 minutes before departure. Wear closed shoes and a warm layer—paths can be wet and slippery. Photography rules vary by tour section.

image.author: Dasha Shishkova
image.attribution: Photo: Dasha Shishkova, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
image.proof_notes: Commons file 'File:Piedra del Peñol.jpg' confirms Guatapé; desc: Esta fotografía fue tomada en el municipio colombiano con código 05321.

facts.one_liner: Lakeside Antioquia town of painted zócalos beside El Peñón de Guatapé (La Piedra del Peñol).
facts.why_go: Guatapé, about 75 km east of Medellín, is known for brightly painted house bases (zócalos) that depict local trades, flora, and history along streets such as Calle del Recuerdo. The Peñol-Guatapé reservoir, created for a hydroelectric project that flooded thousands of hectares in the 1970s, frames boat trips and waterfront walks. Nearby El Peñón de Guatapé—a ~220 m granite monolith between Guatapé and El Peñol—has a stairway of roughly 700 steps to a reservoir overlook.
facts.best_time: Dry season (Dec–Mar) is clearest for the rock climb and photos; Guatapé is visited year-round. Weekdays are less crowded than weekends.
facts.how_to_get_there: Buses run from Medellín’s Terminal del Norte to Guatapé (~2 hours). The rock is on the El Peñol–Guatapé road, a short ride or walk before town. Day tours from Medellín are common.
facts.good_to_know: Bring cash (COP) for the rock entrance and parking; card acceptance on site is unreliable. Climb early morning or late afternoon to avoid heat and peak queues.

facts.one_liner: Bangli highland village with a single stone main street, gated compounds, and a bamboo forest.
facts.why_go: Penglipuran (Desa Wisata Penglipuran) in Kubu, Bangli Regency, is a Bali Aga community noted for its orderly stone-paved main street lined with manicured gardens and traditional arched house gates leading toward the village temple. Visitors can walk residential lanes, enter designated homes, and reach the bamboo forest on the village edge. UN Tourism named it one of the Best Tourism Villages in 2023.
facts.best_time: Dry season (Apr–Oct) for walking comfort; mornings are cooler and less crowded. Closed on Nyepi; may pause for ceremonies.
facts.how_to_get_there: In East Bali’s Bangli highlands, roughly 1–1.5 hours by car from Ubud or south Bali resorts. Address: Jl. Penglipuran, Kubu, Bangli. No public online tickets—buy at the official counter.
facts.good_to_know: From 1 Jan 2026 the village sells visit packages only (not a separate entrance fee) at the official counter; cash IDR or QRIS. Dress modestly; temple inner sanctums are off-limits.

image.attribution: Photo: Mike Maguire, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
image.proof_notes: Commons file 'File:Gásadalur (51256491640).jpg' confirms Gásadalur; desc: The village of Gásadalur in the Faroe Islands. From Wikipedia: Gásadalur is located on the edge of Mykinesfjørður, surrounded by the highest

facts.one_liner: Tiny Vágar cliff village above Múlafossur, a waterfall that drops straight into the Atlantic.
facts.why_go: Gásadalur sits on the west side of Vágar with a handful of houses (official tourism sources cited about 13 residents as of 2023) above sea cliffs. Its landmark is Múlafossur, the waterfall that plunges from the village edge into the ocean, with Mykines visible on clear days. Road access arrived only with the Gásadalstunnilin tunnel in 2005; before that the settlement was reached on foot over the mountains from Bøur.
facts.best_time: May–Sep for longer daylight and milder weather; expect wind and fog any month. Winter visits are possible but weather-dependent.
facts.how_to_get_there: Drive from Vágar Airport or Sørvágur through the tunnel from Bøur (~15–20 min from the airport area). Park only in marked spaces and walk ~5 minutes to the fenced viewpoint. Optional demanding hike: the old postman’s trail from Bøur.
facts.good_to_know: Stay inside fences—cliff terrain is steep and dangerous. Do not drive on turf or block local access. Bring layers; wind at the viewpoint can be strong.

image.author: Hansueli Krapf
image.attribution: Photo: Hansueli Krapf, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
image.proof_notes: Commons file 'File:2007-06-09 Eguisheim 01.jpg' confirms Eguisheim; desc: Exe, Elsàss

facts.one_liner: Concentric Alsace wine village of half-timbered houses on the Route des Vins d’Alsace.
facts.why_go: Eguisheim (Pays d’Eguisheim) is a medieval village near Colmar laid out in concentric streets following former ramparts, notably along Rue du Rempart. Half-timbered façades, flower displays, and Place du Château—with its chapel and statue of Pope Leo IX, traditionally linked to the village—make it a compact walking stop on the Alsace Wine Route. It is listed among Les Plus Beaux Villages de France.
facts.best_time: Apr–Jun for flowers and milder crowds; Sep–Oct for vineyard colour and harvest. Jul–Aug and December Christmas markets are busiest.
facts.how_to_get_there: ~7 km southwest of Colmar (train to Gare de Colmar, then local bus or taxi/bike). By car: A35 exit Sainte-Croix-en-Plaine / Herrlisheim toward Eguisheim. The historic core is walkable (~250 m across).
facts.good_to_know: Tourist office at 22a Grand Rue (Office de Tourisme Pays d’Eguisheim et de Rouffach). Arrive early on weekends; parking fills quickly in high season and around Christmas markets.

image.author: Bernard Gagnon
image.attribution: Photo: Bernard Gagnon, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
image.proof_notes: Commons file 'File:Stari Most viewed from North.jpg' confirms Mostar; desc: Stari Most viewed from Koski Mehmed Pasha Mosque, Mostar, Bosnia and Herzegovina

facts.one_liner: UNESCO Old Bridge (Stari Most) and riverside bazaar spanning the Neretva gorge.
facts.why_go: Mostar’s Old Bridge Area of the Old City is a UNESCO World Heritage property (inscribed 2005) centred on Stari Most, the reconstructed Ottoman stone arch over the Neretva. The surrounding Kujundžiluk bazaar lanes mix Ottoman, Mediterranean, and Austro-Hungarian fabric restored after wartime destruction in the 1990s. Local divers from Klub skakača u vodu Mostari continue the bridge-jumping tradition spectators often watch from the banks in warm months.
facts.best_time: May–Jun and Sep for warm weather with fewer crowds; Jul–Aug is peak for bridge-diving displays and heat. Winter is quiet but cooler and quieter for walking.
facts.how_to_get_there: ŽFBH trains and frequent buses link Sarajevo and Mostar (~2–2.5 hours by rail when running). The old town is compact and walkable from Mostar station/bus terminals with a short walk or taxi to Stari Most.
facts.good_to_know: Crossing Stari Most is free and pedestrian; expect slippery cobbles. Bridge jumps are most reliable roughly Jun–Sep late morning to mid-afternoon—watch from the riverbank, tip if you join a collection, and never jump yourself without club training.

image.author: manuelfloresv
image.attribution: Photo: manuelfloresv, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
image.proof_notes: Commons file 'File:Júzcar Málaga Andalusia Spain smurf town.jpg' confirms Júzcar; desc: Entire town of Júzcar painted blue by Sony Pictures.

facts.one_liner: Blue-painted pueblo in Málaga’s Genal Valley, officially promoted as La Aldea Azul.
facts.why_go: Júzcar is a small municipality in the Serranía de Ronda / Valle del Genal, about 22 km from Ronda. In 2011 its buildings were painted blue for a Smurfs film promotion; residents later voted to keep the colour, and after a rights dispute the place is marketed as La Aldea Azul rather than an official Smurf village. Beyond the blue streets, visitors use it as a base for Genal Valley walks, including autumn chestnut colour in the nearby Bosque de Cobre.
facts.best_time: Spring (Apr–Jun) and autumn (Sep–Nov)—autumn for chestnut (Bosque de Cobre) colour. Summers are hot; winters mild but quieter.
facts.how_to_get_there: Drive MA-515 from Ronda (~30 min) or via inland routes from Málaga (~1.5–2 hours, ~113–115 km). Limited local buses from Ronda to Genal villages—confirm return times. Parking near the village entrance.
facts.good_to_know: Expect the blue paint, not licensed Smurf statues or branding—the village has rebranded toward local nature and chestnut themes. Combine with other Genal white villages if you have a car.

image.author: rboed*
image.attribution: Photo: rboed*, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
image.proof_notes: Commons file 'File:Portree harbour, Isle of Skye, Scotland - 53732030830.jpg' confirms Portree; desc: Portree harbour

facts.one_liner: Skye’s harbour capital (Port Rìgh) on a sheltered bay facing Raasay.
facts.why_go: Portree is the main town and service hub on the Isle of Skye, set around a sheltered harbour on Loch Portree / the Sound of Raasay with brightly painted waterfront buildings and a working pier. Developed as a fishing settlement in the early 19th century, it now concentrates shops, accommodation, and the island’s tourist information, and is a launch point for boat trips and island sightseeing. Hills such as Ben Tianavaig frame the bay; Raasay’s Dun Caan is visible across the water.
facts.best_time: May–Sep for longer days and more services; shoulder months are quieter. Weather is changeable year-round—pack waterproofs.
facts.how_to_get_there: Drive via the free Skye Bridge (Kyle of Lochalsh–Kyleakin), then A87 to Portree (~1 hour from the bridge). Scottish Citylink coaches from Inverness and Glasgow serve Somerled Square; CalMac ferries reach Skye at Armadale (Mallaig) with onward bus. No railway on Skye.
facts.good_to_know: Book Citylink seats in summer. Local Stagecoach buses cover Staffin, Uig, and Dunvegan but run infrequently—check timetables. Harbour pontoon access can close during cruise-ship operations.

image.attribution: Photo: Pavfo, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
image.proof_notes: Commons file 'File:Oia santorini panoramic view overlooking volcano.JPG' confirms Oia; desc: Panoramic view from Oia's cliffs, overlooking the island of Santorini, Thira, Volcano (Palia & Nea Kameni) and beyon

facts.one_liner: Northwest Santorini village on the caldera rim — whitewashed lanes, castle ruins, and sunset crowds.
facts.why_go: Oia (Οία, often spelled Ia; pronounced EE-ah) sits on the northwestern edge of Santorini’s caldera, about 70–100 m above the sea, with white Cycladic houses, blue-domed churches, and windmills along the cliff. Travellers come for caldera views, cave-house stays, and the ruined Kasteli of Agios Nikolaos (Londsa / Oia Castle) at the western tip — a free open-air viewpoint rather than a ticketed fortress. Below the village, Ammoudi Bay is reached by hundreds of steps and offers harbour tavernas and boat links toward Therasia. Nikolaou Nomikou is the main pedestrian spine through shops and galleries.
facts.best_time: April–June and September–October for milder weather and thinner crowds. July–August sunsets at the castle ruins draw dense crowds; mornings are quieter for walking the lanes.
facts.how_to_get_there: Fly or ferry to Santorini, then take the KTEL bus from Fira to Oia (~20 minutes) or a taxi/rental car (parking fills in peak season). The village centre is largely car-free — explore on foot.
facts.good_to_know: Arrive well before sunset if you want space at the castle ruins; otherwise visit earlier for empty lanes and the same caldera views. Optional: the Fira–Oia caldera-rim path ends here if you prefer to walk in rather than bus.

facts.one_liner: Well-preserved Franconian walled town on the Romantic Road with a walkable ~4 km rampart circuit.
facts.why_go: Rothenburg ob der Tauber is a major tourist town in Middle Franconia whose old centre is enclosed by roughly four kilometres of medieval walls and dozens of towers. Visitors walk the Rothenburger Turmweg along the fortifications, pass gates such as Rödertor and Spitaltor, and explore Marktplatz and the Plönlein viewpoint. It sits on Germany’s Romantic Road and draws day-trippers as well as overnight stays in historic inns.
facts.best_time: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct for milder weather; December Christmas market period is busiest. Early morning or evening wall walks avoid peak coach groups.
facts.how_to_get_there: Regional trains to Rothenburg ob der Tauber station (connections via Steinach); short walk or bus into the old town. By car via A7, then local roads; park outside the walls and walk in. Also reachable by Romantic Road buses from other Franconian towns.
facts.good_to_know: Pick up the English Tower Trail brochure at Tourist Information, Marktplatz 2. Much of the wall walk is open around the clock as a footpath; watch uneven stones and steep drops. 2026 theme year: City.Landscape.Nature.

facts.one_liner: Cádiz white town; houses under Río Guadalporcún limestone overhangs (Cuevas del Sol/Sombra).
facts.why_go: Setenil de las Bodegas sits in the Sierra de Cádiz along a narrow river gorge, where façades close natural rock overhangs so the cliff forms much of the roof—semi-troglodyte streets rather than fully carved caves. Visitors walk Cuevas del Sol and Cuevas de la Sombra, then climb to the castle and Iglesia de la Encarnación above the gorge. The historic centre is a declared conjunto histórico-artístico (1985). Olive and almond groves still shape the surrounding landscape; the bodegas that gave the town its name largely vanished after 19th-century phylloxera.
facts.best_time: Spring (March–May) and autumn (September–October) for milder walks in the gorge; summer afternoons are hot. Combine with a Ronda day trip; weekday mornings are quieter than weekend peaks.
facts.how_to_get_there: About 15–20 minutes by road from Ronda, ~90 minutes from Málaga or Cádiz by car. No train station—arrive by car or regional bus via Ronda/Olvera. Park on the upper town and walk down into the cave streets.
facts.good_to_know: The rock is the roof of many buildings: Cuevas del Sol is the sunnier, café-lined stretch; Cuevas de la Sombra stays cooler. Stay on public streets—many openings are still homes or shops.

facts.one_liner: Phlegraean island near Naples; Marina Corricella pastel fishing harbour, car-free quay.
facts.why_go: Procida (Proceta) is a small Campanian island between Capo Miseno and Ischia, with ~10,000 residents and a working maritime character. People come for Marina Corricella—an amphitheatre of multicoloured façades above a vehicle-free fishing quay—plus Terra Murata, the fortified hilltop settlement. Ferries land at Marina Grande; Corricella is reached only by sea or stairways such as Gradinata del Pennino and Gradinata Scura. Procida was Italian Capital of Culture in 2022.
facts.best_time: May–June and September–October for warm weather and lighter crowds. July–August are busiest with domestic holidays; winter services run but are fewer.
facts.how_to_get_there: Hydrofoil (~35–40 min) from Naples Molo Beverello or ferry (~1 h) from Calata Porta di Massa; also frequent boats from Pozzuoli. All arrive at Marina Grande. No airport—use Napoli Capodichino then port transfer.
facts.good_to_know: Corricella has no cars; expect stairs and narrow lanes. Check Caremar/SNAV times the day before—rough seas can cancel hydrofoils. Overnight stays beat same-day Capri-style day trips.

facts.one_liner: Cinque Terre hamlet in Riomaggiore; cliffside tower-houses above a tiny rocky harbour.
facts.why_go: Manarola is one Cinque Terre village—a frazione of Riomaggiore (La Spezia)—not a stand-in for all five towns. Tall, narrow painted houses rise from a steep cliff around a small harbour used for boats, rock swimming, and diving rather than a sandy beach. Vineyards and olive terraces climb the slopes above; recorded settlement ties to the 13th-century Fieschi period. Within Cinque Terre National Park and the Porto Venere–Cinque Terre UNESCO coastal site, it is best explored on foot via carruggi and slate stairs.
facts.best_time: April–June and September–October for hiking weather and fewer peak crowds. Midsummer trains and paths are heavily loaded; winter is quieter with shorter ferry seasons.
facts.how_to_get_there: Regional trains on the Genova–La Spezia line stop at Manarola station above the village; walk downhill into the centre (steep). Seasonal Line 02 ferries (Navigazione Golfo dei Poeti) call at the harbour when seas allow. Cars are restricted—park outside and walk or use the train.
facts.good_to_know: Focus on Manarola’s harbour viewpoint (Via Belvedere) and village lanes; trail links (including Via dell’Amore segments) need current park status and often timed tickets. Buy the Cinque Terre Card if using trains heavily between villages.

facts.one_liner: UNESCO trading-port old town on the Thu Bồn; timber shophouses, Japanese Covered Bridge.
facts.why_go: Hội An Ancient Town (Hội An) in Quảng Nam preserves a compact riverside trading port active from roughly the 15th–19th centuries, inscribed by UNESCO in 1999. Visitors come for timber shophouses, Chinese assembly halls, museums, and the Japanese Covered Bridge (Chùa Cầu), plus lantern-lit evening streets. The core is small and walkable; an official heritage ticket covers selected monuments. Pedestrian and non-motorized vehicle rules apply in the historic streets for much of the day.
facts.best_time: February–April is the driest, most comfortable window per local heritage guidance. May–August is hotter but often still dry; September–December brings heavier rain and possible flooding.
facts.how_to_get_there: No airport or railway in Hoi An. Fly into Da Nang (DAD), ~30 km / 45–60 minutes by taxi, Grab, shuttle, or public bus. Hue and Mỹ Sơn are common day trips.
facts.good_to_know: Buy the official entrance ticket at authorised booths before touring ticketed sites; keep the stub for re-entry checks. Dress modestly inside temples and historic houses; the old town is a lived-in neighbourhood, not a closed museum.

facts.one_liner: Townsite inside Banff National Park; Bow Valley base for lakes, trails, and Roam transit.
facts.why_go: Banff is a small mountain town (~4 km²) inside Banff National Park in Alberta’s Canadian Rockies, about 128 km west of Calgary. Visitors use the townsite as a walkable base for park attractions—Bow Falls, Sulphur Mountain gondola, Cave and Basin, Lake Minnewanka, Johnston Canyon, and day access toward Lake Louise—rather than treating “the Rockies” as a generic backdrop. Parks Canada manages the park; the Town of Banff runs local services and strongly encourages car-free travel once you arrive.
facts.best_time: June–September for hiking and lake access; September–October for fall colour and thinner crowds; winter for snow sports and quieter streets. Summer parking fills early on clear days.
facts.how_to_get_there: Fly to Calgary (YYC), then ~1.5 hours by highway, airport shuttle, or scheduled bus (e.g. Banff Airporter, Brewster Express, FlixBus). Inside Banff, walk, cycle, or use Roam Public Transit to town and major park stops.
facts.good_to_know: A national park pass is normally required for park entry (check Parks Canada for current rules). Downtown and attraction lots often fill by ~10:00 in peak summer—arrive late afternoon or leave the car at your lodging and use Roam.

facts.one_liner: UNESCO mudbrick ksar in Ouarzazate Province; Ounila Valley earthen fortified village.
facts.why_go: Aït Benhaddou (Ksar of Ait-Ben-Haddou; آيت بن حدّو) is a fortified earthen village (ksar/ighrem) on the southern High Atlas slopes in Ouarzazate Province, inscribed by UNESCO in 1987. High defensive walls with corner towers enclose packed dwellings of rammed earth and adobe—an exemplary pre-Saharan building tradition on a former caravan route toward Marrakesh. Most residents now live across the river in the modern village; a pedestrian bridge links the two. The site has also served as a film location (e.g. Gladiator, parts of Game of Thrones), which is secondary to its architectural value.
facts.best_time: October–April for cooler walking temperatures. Summer midday heat is intense; early morning or late afternoon is better for climbing to the granary viewpoint. After heavy rain, earthen paths can be slippery.
facts.how_to_get_there: About 30 km / 30–40 minutes from Ouarzazate by grand taxi or tour. From Marrakesh, allow roughly 4 hours via the Tizi n’Tichka road, usually as a day trip or overnight with Ouarzazate. No train—road only.
facts.good_to_know: Wear closed shoes for uneven mudbrick alleys and the hilltop climb. Guides and some individual buildings may charge separately; confirm current access after any regional weather or seismic events. This is not Chefchaouen—expect ochre earth walls, not blue medina lanes.

facts.one_liner: Basilicata city of the Sassi; UNESCO cave districts and rupestrian churches.
facts.why_go: Matera’s historic core is famous for the Sassi—dense districts of cave dwellings and stone façades cut into the Gravina gorge—together with the Park of the Rupestrian Churches, inscribed by UNESCO in 1993. People visit to walk Sasso Caveoso and Sasso Barisano, enter rock-hewn churches, and see how a once-stigmatized cave city became a major cultural destination (European Capital of Culture 2019). Exploration is almost entirely on foot: steep lanes, stairs, and uneven stone. The “new town” above provides hotels and parking outside restricted zones.
facts.best_time: April–May and September–October for mild walking weather. July–August are hot on exposed stone; winter is quieter with shorter daylight.
facts.how_to_get_there: Nearest major airport Bari Palese (~60 km) with shuttles. From Bari Centrale, Ferrovie Appulo Lucane (FAL) to Matera Centrale (~100 min; limited/no trains on some holidays—buses substitute). Long-distance coaches serve Rome, Naples, and other cities. By car, use marked lots and respect the Sassi ZTL.
facts.good_to_know: Wear grippy shoes; many lanes are polished stone. Some cave churches and museums need tickets. Overnight stays let you see the Sassi lit after day-trippers leave.

facts.one_liner: South Bohemia UNESCO town on a Vltava bend; castle complex and medieval centre.
facts.why_go: Český Krumlov (formerly also Krumau) sits on a double bend of the Vltava in South Bohemia. Its historic centre and the large State Castle and Chateau complex—one of the Czech Republic’s major castle sites—form a UNESCO World Heritage property inscribed in 1992. Visitors walk the old town lanes, cross Lazebnický most, and tour castle courtyards, interiors (seasonal guided routes), and the Baroque theatre when open. Day-trip pressure from Prague is high; overnight stays change the evening atmosphere.
facts.best_time: Castle interiors and gardens generally run April–October. May–September are busiest; April and October balance open attractions with fewer crowds. Winter is quiet; some interiors close.
facts.how_to_get_there: Direct buses from Prague (~3 hours) are the simplest. Trains usually require a change at České Budějovice (~4 hours total); the station is a walk or short bus from the centre. Park in designated lots—the historic core is largely pedestrian.
facts.good_to_know: Book castle guided tours ahead in peak season. The centre climbs steeply toward the castle; cobbles are uneven. Infocentrum on náměstí Svornosti handles tickets and local advice.

facts.one_liner: Hunan riverside old town (凤凰古城); Tuojiang stilt houses, Miao–Tujia heritage.
facts.why_go: Fenghuang Ancient Town (凤凰古城, Fènghuáng Gǔchéng—“Phoenix” Ancient Town) in Fenghuang County, Xiangxi, Hunan, lines the Tuojiang (Tuo River) with Ming–Qing–style streets and wooden stilt houses (diaojiaolou). Visitors walk flagstone lanes, ride boats past riverside façades, and see Miao and Tujia cultural life in and around the county. The historic townscape has been on UNESCO’s Tentative List (Fenghuang Ancient City) since 2008—it is not yet a full World Heritage inscription. Night lighting along the river is a major draw; mornings are calmer.
facts.best_time: April–June and September–November for milder weather. Avoid China’s Golden Week peaks (early May, early October) if you can. Winter is quieter and colder; snow is possible.
facts.how_to_get_there: High-speed rail to Fenghuang Ancient Town Station (凤凰古城站), then local shuttle or taxi into the old town. Common gateways: Changsha (~2–3 h by rail) or Zhangjiajie (~1 h). No major airport in the town itself.
facts.good_to_know: Street walking is generally free; combo tickets cover selected heritage sites and daytime boat rides—night cruises are often sold separately. Stay overnight for dawn mist and evening lights; expect stairs and damp stone after rain.

facts.one_liner: Hill town of Romantic palaces in UNESCO Cultural Landscape near Lisbon.
facts.why_go: Sintra sits on the wooded Serra de Sintra west of Lisbon and forms the Cultural Landscape of Sintra, inscribed by UNESCO in 1995 as an early centre of European Romantic architecture. Visitors come for the Park and National Palace of Pena, the Moorish Castle, the National Palace of Sintra in the historic centre, and related estates such as Monserrate and Quinta da Regaleira. Parques de Sintra manages timed tickets and park access; private cars are not authorised on the roads to Pena and the Moorish Castle, so buses or walking trails are the practical last link.
facts.best_time: Spring and autumn for milder weather and thinner queues; summer is peak and hottest. Book Pena and other Parques de Sintra tickets ahead, especially weekends.
facts.how_to_get_there: CP Sintra Line train from Lisbon (Rossio, Oriente, or Entrecampos) to Sintra station. Scotturb bus 434 links the station/Lourel car park with Pena and the Moorish Castle; buses 434/435 serve the National Palace area. Park at peripheral lots such as Lourel—historic-centre driving is restricted.
facts.good_to_know: Allow a full day if combining Pena Park (walk time from park gate to palace) with the Moorish Castle. Wear good shoes for hills and cobbles; check Parques de Sintra for current shuttle and access rules.

facts.one_liner: Car-free Valais village under the Matterhorn, reached by train via Täsch.
facts.why_go: Zermatt is a car-free mountain village in Valais known for its setting beneath the Matterhorn (4,478 m), which can be seen from points in the village such as the church square. Guests come for alpine hiking and skiing, Bahnhofstrasse, and high viewpoints including Gornergrat, Sunnegga, and Rothorn. The Gornergrat Bahn cogwheel railway starts opposite Zermatt station and reaches Gornergrat (~3,100 m) in about 33 minutes for a classic Matterhorn panorama among surrounding 4,000 m peaks.
facts.best_time: Winter for skiing on linked Matterhorn areas; summer/early autumn for hiking with long daylight. Shoulder months are quieter than school-holiday peaks.
facts.how_to_get_there: Private cars stop at Täsch (~5 km before Zermatt). Park at Matterhorn Terminal Täsch (covered spaces) and take the Matterhorn Gotthard Bahn shuttle (~12 minutes, frequent) into central Zermatt, or use a licensed taxi. Direct trains also run into Zermatt from the Swiss network (roughly 3.5–4 hours from major airports).
facts.good_to_know: Unauthorised driving into Zermatt risks fines. In town, walk, e-bus, e-taxi, or bicycle. Matterhorn climbing is for experienced alpinists only—most visitors enjoy views from village or mountain railways.

facts.one_liner: Rajasthan’s Blue City of indigo-washed lanes beneath Mehrangarh Fort.
facts.why_go: Jodhpur, Rajasthan’s second-largest city, is widely called the Blue City because many houses, havelis, and temples in the old quarter are painted vivid blue, especially below the fort ridge. Mehrangarh Fort—begun under Rao Jodha in 1459 and still managed by the Mehrangarh Museum Trust—dominates the skyline and holds palace museums with Marwar collections. Nearby Jaswant Thada, a white marble memorial completed in 1906, is a common pairing with the fort visit.
facts.best_time: October–March for cooler daytime temperatures; summers are very hot. Early morning or late afternoon for old-city walks and fort views.
facts.how_to_get_there: Jodhpur has rail, road, and airport links within Rajasthan and from major Indian cities. The blue-washed lanes and Mehrangarh sit in/above the old city; autorickshaws and taxis reach the fort approaches—confirm current vehicle restrictions near the gates.
facts.good_to_know: Mehrangarh Museum is listed open daily 09:00–17:00; timed online tickets are advised by the Trust. Modest dress and water are useful in the old city; midday heat is intense outside winter.

facts.one_liner: Chilean port of hillside cerros, murals, and UNESCO-listed elevators.
facts.why_go: Valparaíso’s Historic Quarter of the Seaport City was inscribed by UNESCO in 2003 for its amphitheatre-like layout of port plain and steep hills (cerros), late-19th-century architecture, and industrial funicular elevators (ascensores). Cerro Alegre and Cerro Concepción are the best-known visitor hills, with paseos, stairways, murals, and elevator links such as El Peral, Concepción, and Reina Victoria. The working port and street art culture remain central to why travellers stay overnight rather than only day-trip from Santiago.
facts.best_time: Chilean summer (Dec–Mar) for longer days; spring and autumn are milder. Foggy mornings (camanchaca) are common year-round on the coast.
facts.how_to_get_there: About 120 km west of Santiago via Route 68 (~1.5 hours by bus or car). From the Valparaíso bus terminal, taxis or short rides reach central elevators; walking between hills is steep.
facts.good_to_know: Carry small cash for elevator tickets and wear shoes with grip. Petty theft can occur in crowded areas—keep bags closed. Several elevators operate intermittently; Chile Travel lists Concepción, Artillería, El Peral, and Reina Victoria among heritage links to Alegre/Concepción.

facts.one_liner: Jujuy adobe town at the foot of Cerro de los Siete Colores.
facts.why_go: Purmamarca is a small adobe town in Jujuy Province at about 2,195 m, known for sitting beside Cerro de los Siete Colores (Seven Colors Hill / Seven Colours Hill). The village lies in the Quebrada de Humahuaca cultural landscape, inscribed by UNESCO in 2003 along the Río Grande corridor. Travellers come for the coloured sedimentary slopes visible from town, the Paseo de los Colorados walk behind the hill, craft markets, and as a base for the wider quebrada (Tilcara, Humahuaca, and related stops).
facts.best_time: Austral autumn and spring for clearer skies and milder nights; winter mornings can be cold at altitude. Summer brings more rain in the northwest Andes.
facts.how_to_get_there: About 65 km (~1 hour) from San Salvador de Jujuy via RN 9 then RN 52 (Purmamarca sits ~3 km west of RN 9 on RN 52). Regular buses leave from the new bus terminal in San Salvador de Jujuy roughly hourly from early morning into evening.
facts.good_to_know: Cerro de los Siete Colores is the local/provincial name for the landmark hill; it is not a separate UNESCO listing from Quebrada de Humahuaca. The Paseo de los Colorados is a ~3 km circuit with an entrance fee; altitude and sun call for water and layers. Local forms: Cerro de los Siete Colores / Seven Colors Hill.

facts.one_liner: 1980 Popeye film set at Anchor Bay, still open as a Malta attraction.
facts.why_go: Popeye Village (also called Sweethaven) at Anchor Bay near Mellieħa is the preserved wooden set built for the 1980 Robert Altman film Popeye, now run as a family visitor attraction. Guests walk the film-set streets overlooking the bay, see shows and museum/documentary content, and—depending on season—use water play areas and mini-golf. It is a purpose-built attraction rather than a historic Maltese village, distinct from Mdina or Valletta.
facts.best_time: Shoulder months for milder weather; high season (Jun–Sep) adds water features but is hottest and busiest. Open daily year-round per the operator’s seasonal calendar.
facts.how_to_get_there: On Malta’s northwest coast at Anchor Bay (Il-Bajja tal-Mellieħa area). Reachable by car, taxi, or local bus connections toward Mellieħa/Anchor Bay; check current routes from Valletta or northern resorts.
facts.good_to_know: As of the operator’s published 2026 calendar, Popeye Village remains open as a ticketed attraction (low/mid/high seasons with different hours and packages). Book online to skip queues; confirm hours before travel as seasonal offerings change.

facts.one_liner: Alpine lake with island church and cliff-top castle in Upper Carniola.
facts.why_go: Bled (Blejsko jezero) is an Alpine resort in Upper Carniola on the edge of Triglav National Park, known for its lake, cliff-top Bled Castle (Blejski grad), and the only natural island in Slovenia. Travellers take a traditional pletna boat to Bled Island (Blejski otok) and climb 99 stone steps to the Church of the Mother of God on the Lake (Cerkev Marijinega vnebovzetja), with a wishing bell and lookout bell tower. The lakeshore path and cream cake (kremšnita) culture make it a short stay or day trip from Ljubljana.
facts.best_time: May–September for boating and swimming weather; autumn colours are strong. Winter is quieter; island buildings keep seasonal hours.
facts.how_to_get_there: About 55 km northwest of Ljubljana by road or bus. Pletna boats leave from lakeside points (e.g. Kazina, Mlino, Vila Bled, Velika Zaka); electric boat lines and small boats are also available. Castle access is by foot, bike, or nearby parking then a steep walk.
facts.good_to_know: Island entrance fees (church, bell tower, museum) are separate from boat hire—check blejskiotok.si for 2026 prices and hours. Only rowing/electric boats are used on the lake to protect the setting; bring cash for some lakeside services.

facts.one_liner: Li River karst town known for the vista on China’s ¥20 note.
facts.why_go: Xingping (兴坪; Xīngpíng) is a riverside town in Yangshuo County, Guangxi, on the Li River (漓江; Lí Jiāng) amid classic fengcong/fenglin karst peaks. It is a long-established river town with an old stone street and nearby fishing village architecture, and a common stop on Guilin–Yangshuo river trips. The Li River scenery just outside Xingping is the landscape featured on China’s fifth-series 20-yuan (¥20) banknote—often photographed from riverside viewpoints near town.
facts.best_time: April–May and September–November for clearer air and comfortable hiking; summer is hot and humid with more rain. Early morning for mist and lighter crowds.
facts.how_to_get_there: About 25–30 km from Yangshuo town; direct buses from Yangshuo Bus Station (~30–45 minutes). Yangshuo Railway Station sits near Xingping, with short shuttles into town. Guilin–Xingping buses also run; Li River cruises and Yangdi–Xingping rafts approach from the water.
facts.good_to_know: The ancient town streets are generally free to wander; some riverside viewpoints may charge a small local fee—confirm on site. Bring WeChat/Alipay or cash. Do not confuse with Xingping city in Shaanxi Province.

facts.one_liner: Atlantic medina of Vauban-style ramparts, distinct from inland Morocco.
facts.why_go: Essaouira (الصويرة; formerly Mogador) is an Atlantic fortified town whose Medina was inscribed by UNESCO in 2001 as a mid-18th-century seaport planned with European military (Vauban-influenced) walls in a North African setting. Visitors walk the ramparts and Skala, the working fishing port, and the white-and-blue medina alleys—often cooler and windier than inland cities. It is a coastal medina, not the blue mountain town of Chefchaouen and not the inland ksar of Aït Benhaddou.
facts.best_time: Spring and autumn for milder temperatures; summer is popular for wind sports but can be crowded. The alizé wind is frequent year-round.
facts.how_to_get_there: On Morocco’s Atlantic coast west of Marrakesh (coach ~2.5–3.5 hours depending on service). Domestic flights and coastal buses also serve the area; the medina is largely walkable once you arrive.
facts.good_to_know: Expect strong sea wind on the ramparts—secure hats and cameras. The UNESCO property is the Medina (and associated Mogador archipelago context), not the whole modern city. Local and French forms: Essaouira / الصويرة; historic name Mogador.

facts.one_liner: Walled Bay of Kotor old town in Montenegro’s UNESCO bay landscape.
facts.why_go: Kotor (Котор) sits at the head of Boka Kotorska (Bay of Kotor) on Montenegro’s Adriatic coast. Its fortified old town of stone squares, churches, and alleys is part of the Natural and Culturo-Historical Region of Kotor, a UNESCO World Heritage property covering the inner bay’s historic settlements and mountain backdrop. Visitors walk the walled centre, climb toward the fortress/walls above town, and use Kotor as a base for Perast and boat trips on the bay.
facts.best_time: May–June and September–October for warm weather with fewer cruise-ship crowds than midsummer. Winter is quieter and wetter.
facts.how_to_get_there: Closest major airport is Tivat (TIV), a short coastal transfer to Kotor; Podgorica is farther inland. Buses and cars use the bay road; cruise ships dock near the old town in season.
facts.good_to_know: The UNESCO listing covers the wider bay cultural landscape (including towns such as Kotor and Perast), not only the old-town walls. Expect steep stairs if ascending the fortifications; mornings before ship excursions are quieter in peak season. Local forms: Kotor / Котор; Boka Kotorska / Bay of Kotor.
